# Recycle your tests: many shades of green


”Our environment is under constant pressure, and all we want is to see more green.” I say this sentence quite often at work, and it has never had anything to do with the planet.


In a[previous article](https://tech.trivago.com/post/2026-04-15-my-2-cents-ill-gladly-spend-them-to-stop-staring-at-test-logs) , I mentioned that test failures pile up when the environment has a bad day. This time, the environment is the topic, in both senses. Here’s how we took a small subset of the end-to-end tests we already maintain and gave them three new jobs:


- monitoring our live platforms
- collecting performance data after each release
- checking stage stability after backend changes


All three run on scenarios we had already written and were maintaining anyway.


## The hidden waste of single-purpose tests


End-to-end tests are expensive. They are expensive to write, to keep stable, and to run. A scenario that searches for a destination, applies a filter and checks the results can take several iterations to get right and make as bulletproof as possible. Then it lives the life of a jam jar that only ever holds jam: useful, refilled on every pull request, but never considered for anything else. Anyone who has seen a kitchen shelf knows jars can do a lot more.


The CI that orchestrates our tests’ execution with internally developed, Selenium-based framework, trupi, runs these scenarios in two layers: a small core suite on every commit and a larger extended suite on demand. The easily configurable control layer resides in the Cucumber tags that we point CI to. Just run` @core and not @skipdesktop` tag expression and the correct set of tests get executed. Every one of those scenarios already knows how to use trivago the way a traveler would. All that development and refinement effort has been done over time. So we asked ourselves: what else could they be doing between pull requests? And then other teams asked us similar questions: could your test automation framework also do “this”? Bringing new requirements and ideas to the table.


## Sorting the bins


Living in Germany teaches you waste separation early: paper, packaging, glass, organic, residual. Try to read everything about[“Mülltrennung”](https://www.swd-ag.de/magazin/wohnen/muelltrennung/) in Düsseldorf, our city, and you’ll figure out it’s a quite complex setup. And don’t get me started on bottle deposits. It turns out tests can be sorted the same way.


Trupi scenarios are written in Gherkin, and tags already decide where each one runs. For example` @core` runs on every commit,` @extended` runs on demand. A tag is a chance to re-use a test. To give a scenario a new life, we add a tag. The test code stays as it is.


```text
@live
@core
@trupi.plugin.graphqlcallcount.enabled:true
@trupi.chromium_enableFullPerformanceLogs:true
@trupi.chromium_logLevel:info
Scenario  :   Core search flow from homepage
Given   I am on the homepage
When   I type   'bangkok'   into the search field
Then   I see that the SSG item in position 1 is   'Bangkok'
When   I select the SSG item in position 1
...
```


## Bin one: synthetic monitoring


This is a re-use that we identified already long ago, consistently in place for years. Two` @live` scenarios run against production every 10 minutes. They run in GitHub Actions, but they’re currently triggered by an external scheduler maintained by our DX team, to guarantee consistent execution independently from GitHub. They point at three GCP regions and test some of our platforms (trivago.co.uk, trivago.com, and trivago.co.kr) using proxies to appear as a local visitor. Failure notifications land in a dedicated Slack channel, supporting our SREs efforts to keep the platform not only up at all times, but also actually usable by final customers.


You could call this downcycling. These scenarios somehow do less than their CI siblings. The question is no longer “does this feature behave as specified?” but “are the lights on, everywhere, right now?”


There’s also some responsible waste separation involved. All automated traffic carries an automation identifier, so test executions never counted in our analytics and don’t pollute calculations by our Search Intelligence. We sort our own waste so it doesn’t end up in someone else’s bin.


And there’s one trap to avoid: greenwashing. A synthetic monitor that is always green because it barely asserts anything is worse than no monitor at all, because it gives you confidence you haven’t earned. Each live scenario checks something that would really matter to a traveler, such as results showing up and prices being present on all accommodations. Not every shade of green is worth the same. When a live scenario is green, it has to mean something.


## Bin two: performance data after each release


After each release of our web application, the same scenarios run against the stage deployment again. This time they also collect some metrics about what we actually deliver to the browser of our users, for example the size of CSS, images, JavaScript and network calls to our GraphQL gateway. We put those under a sort of RUM metrics definition.


Yes, this is Real User Monitoring data from a user who isn’t real, and that’s exactly why it’s useful. Real user data needs traffic to build up, and it varies with every device, network, and browser out there. Our synthetic user takes the same journey on the same setup on the same environment after every release. When a number moves, the release is the most likely cause. Think of it as lab data sitting next to field data. It doesn’t replace the real user metrics in our Release Controller, which are thoroughly collected from actual visitors, but it gives an early and consistent first reading.


If the first bin was downcycling, this one is upcycling. It’s the same run, with more value on top.


## Bin three: stage stability after backend changes


The third re-use points the same suites at our stage environment right after backend changes, through an internal system that automates various operational workflows based on hooks from systems like GitHub, ArgoCD, and Rootly. The goal is to alert about environment instability and potentially also catch integration problems before they reach production and before developers lose time on failures that aren’t theirs.


This is also where the metaphor gets honest: recycling has a carbon footprint too. Stage doesn’t have the capacity of production, and as test volume grew across backend, gateway and frontend, we saw what the costs are. Responses slowed down, searches sometimes returned no results, and overnight runs were noticeably more stable than daytime ones. Our tests were, quite literally, polluting the environment they were meant to check. The lesson is to recycle selectively: run what you need, where you need it, and not everything everywhere.


## What makes a test recyclable


Not every scenario deserves a second life. The ones that work well share a few traits:


- **Configurable targets:** the base URL, region, and device come from configuration, not from the code.
- **No side effects:** they use dedicated test accounts and marked traffic, and they never change real data.
- **Safe to repeat:** they run every 10 minutes without leaving anything behind.
- **Meaningful assertions:** green has to mean something (see greenwashing above).
- **Visible failures:** results go to a channel where a human will actually see them.
- **Small and fast:** a few reliable scenarios beat a large, flaky collection.


## Conclusion


My nonna never threw away stale bread. It became panzanella, or “[Pisarei e faśö](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pisarei_e_fa%C5%9B%C3%B6) ”, a lesser-known recipe from her city, and nobody complained. A well-built end-to-end scenario deserves the same respect: it is worth checking what it can do after its main job is done. Sorting ours with a few tags gave them three new jobs: watching production, measuring each release, and checking stage, with very little new code. Just remember that recycling also costs energy, so choose carefully what goes into each bin. Before you write your next test, check the bins first.
